shots.line: June first, two thousand nine. It's the middle of the night over the Atlantic Ocean.
shots.scene: Night over the Atlantic, an airliner above the storms

shots.line: An Airbus A three-thirty is flying from Rio de Janeiro to Paris, with two hundred and twenty-eight people on board.
shots.scene: Map: Rio to Paris, 228 people

shots.line: Somewhere far from any coast, the plane flies into a region of thunderstorms.
shots.scene: The plane flies into a region of thunderstorms

shots.line: And then, it simply stops reporting. No mayday. No warning call. Nothing.
shots.scene: It stops reporting: no mayday, no warning, nothing

shots.line: Search teams find wreckage on the surface within days.
shots.scene: Search planes over the ocean, wreckage on the surface

shots.line: But the most important question has no answer. A modern jet, flown by an experienced crew, fell out of the sky. Why?
shots.scene: A modern jet, an experienced crew... why?

shots.line: The answer is lying almost four kilometers below the surface, in two small orange boxes. And it will take almost two years to reach them.
shots.scene: Descending to the sea floor: two orange boxes, ~4 km down

shots.line: Stay with me, because by the end of this video, you'll know exactly what those boxes revealed, and how one tiny frozen sensor started it all.
shots.scene: Freeze on the boxes: what did they reveal?

shots.line: This is the story of the black box.
shots.scene: Title: INSIDE THE BLACK BOX

shots.line: First, let's clear something up. The black box isn't black. It's bright orange, often with reflective stripes, so searchers can spot it in wreckage, in a forest, or on the bottom of the ocean.
shots.scene: Myth: the black box is orange

shots.line: So why the name? Nobody knows for sure. Some say the very first versions were painted black. Some say "black box" was simply old slang for any mysterious electronic gadget. Others say it's because the boxes were found scorched and charred after a fire. Take your pick.
shots.scene: Theories behind the name

shots.line: And here's the second surprise. It isn't one box. It's two.
shots.scene: It isn't one box. It's two.

shots.line: The first is the cockpit voice recorder. It records everything the pilots say, every radio call, every alarm, every click of a switch, through microphones in their headsets and one in the cockpit itself.
shots.scene: CVR: everything heard in the cockpit

shots.line: The second is the flight data recorder. It quietly logs the plane's measurements, many times every second: speed, altitude, engine power, the position of every control. Modern recorders can track well over a thousand of them.
shots.scene: FDR: data streams from all over the plane

shots.line: Think of it like this. Every second of every flight becomes a long row of numbers. String those rows together, and you get a perfect digital record of everything the plane did, from push back to parking.
shots.scene: Every second becomes a row of numbers

items.s: EVERY SECOND = ONE ROW OF NUMBERS

shots.line: After an accident, investigators feed those numbers into a computer and rebuild the flight as an animation, matched to the sounds from the cockpit. They can watch exactly where the plane went, what the controls did, and what the crew heard, moment by moment.
shots.scene: The numbers become a replay of the flight

shots.line: That work is done by independent investigators, like the NTSB in the United States, the BEA in France, or the AAIB in the U.K. And their job isn't to blame anyone. It's to find out what happened, so it can't happen again.
shots.scene: Independent investigators: safety, not blame

shots.line: Together, they can rebuild the final minutes of a flight almost second by second.
shots.scene: Together: the final minutes, second by second

items.s: THE FINAL MINUTES, SECOND BY SECOND

shots.line: Quick question before we go on. Where on the plane do you think the recorders are kept? The nose, the middle, or the tail? Keep your answer in mind. We'll find out in a few minutes.
shots.scene: Quiz: where are the recorders kept?

shots.line: But someone had to invent them first. And it started with a boy who lost his father.
shots.scene: Someone had to invent them: a boy who lost his father

ov.text: A BOY WHO LOST HIS FATHER

shots.line: Nineteen thirty-four.
shots.scene: 1934: sepia flashback over the sea

shots.line: In Australia, a young boy named David Warren loses his father in a plane crash over the sea.
shots.scene: Young David Warren, who loses his father

ov.text: LOSES HIS FATHER IN A PLANE CRASH

shots.line: Nobody ever finds out exactly what happened.
shots.scene: The empty sea: no answers

shots.line: Almost twenty years later, Warren is a scientist at an aeronautical research lab in Melbourne.
shots.scene: Melbourne lab: Warren is now a scientist

shots.line: And the aviation world has a terrifying new mystery: the de Havilland Comet, the world's first jet airliner, is breaking apart in mid-air.
shots.scene: Newspaper: the Comet jets are breaking apart

shots.line: The cause turned out to be metal fatigue. Every flight, the cabin was pressurized and then released, flexing the metal again and again. And the sharp corners around some openings concentrated that stress until cracks spread. It's a big part of why airliner windows today have rounded corners.
shots.scene: Metal fatigue: stress at sharp corners, cracks; round windows

shots.line: Warren is asked to help think about why.
shots.scene: The investigation meeting

shots.line: And sitting in that meeting, he has a simple idea.
shots.scene: Warren gets a simple idea

shots.line: What if the cockpit had a recorder? What if investigators could hear the last words of the crew, and know exactly what the instruments were saying?
shots.scene: What if the cockpit had a recorder?

items.s: WHAT IF THE COCKPIT HAD A RECORDER?

shots.line: At the time, there were already some flight recorders, but they captured only a few basic measurements. Warren wanted something that would capture the voices, too.
shots.scene: Existing recorders captured a few basics; Warren wanted voices

shots.line: By the late nineteen fifties, he had built a working prototype. It could record hours of cockpit sound and instrument readings, and it was small enough to fit in a plane.
shots.scene: Late 1950s: a working prototype

shots.line: It stored about four hours of sound and instrument data on a spool of thin steel wire, recording over itself again and again, so it always held the most recent hours.
shots.scene: 4 hours on steel wire, recording over itself

shots.line: And almost nobody wanted it. Some officials couldn't see the point.
shots.scene: Almost nobody wanted it

shots.line: And pilots hated the idea of a microphone recording everything they said. One complaint stuck: it was like having a spy in the cockpit.
shots.scene: Pilots: "a spy in the cockpit"

shots.line: Warren didn't give up. Interest grew in Britain, where an early commercial version was built. Then, after a deadly crash in Australia in nineteen sixty left investigators with no answers, Australia became one of the first countries to require cockpit recorders on airliners.
shots.scene: Britain builds a version; after a 1960 crash, Australia requires them

items.s: AUSTRALIA: AMONG THE FIRST TO REQUIRE THEM

shots.line: Over the following decades, the rest of the world followed. Today, every large airliner carries both recorders.
shots.scene: The world follows: every large airliner

shots.line: And the pilots' worry about a spy in the cockpit was taken seriously. In many countries, cockpit voice recordings are legally protected. They're used for safety investigations, not to listen in on pilots, and the actual audio is very rarely made public.
shots.scene: Recordings are legally protected

shots.line: The boy who never learned why his father's plane went down ended up making sure that, for countless families after him, there would usually be an answer.
shots.scene: Warren, older, beside a modern orange recorder

shots.line: But a recorder is useless if it doesn't survive the crash. So how do you build a box that can't be destroyed?
shots.scene: Teaser: can a box survive a crash?

items.s: A BOX THAT CAN'T BE DESTROYED?

shots.line: Here's the trick. Most of a black box is protection. The part that actually matters, the memory, is a small, heavily armored core in the middle, wrapped in layers of insulation and steel or titanium.
shots.scene: Cutaway: mostly protection, an armored memory core

shots.line: And before a design is approved, it's put through tests that sound almost cruel.
shots.scene: Tests that sound almost cruel

shots.line: Test one: impact. The box is fired at a target so it stops with a force of about three thousand four hundred times gravity.
shots.scene: Test 1: impact, ~3,400 G

shots.line: Test two: a heavy steel spike is dropped onto it, to make sure nothing sharp in a crash can punch through.
shots.scene: Test 2: a steel spike dropped on it

shots.line: Test three: it's crushed under a press with tons of force, for minutes at a time.
shots.scene: Test 3: crushed under a press

shots.line: Test four: fire. Jet fuel burns hot, so the box is blasted with flames of more than a thousand degrees Celsius for up to an hour.
shots.scene: Test 4: fire, 1,000+ °C for up to an hour

shots.line: Test five: the deep ocean. It's held under pressure like the bottom of the sea, around six kilometers down, for a month, to prove the water and the pressure can't get in.
shots.scene: Test 5: deep-ocean pressure, ~6 km, a month

shots.line: And there's more. It's soaked in jet fuel, hydraulic fluid, and fire-fighting chemicals, all the nasty liquids that can end up around a crash site, to make sure none of them can eat their way inside.
shots.scene: Test 6: soaked in jet fuel, hydraulic fluid, foam

shots.line: Only if the memory inside still reads perfectly afterwards does the design pass.
shots.scene: Only if the memory reads perfectly does it pass

shots.line: And remember my question? Even where they sit is part of the plan. The recorders are usually mounted near the tail, because in many crashes the back of the aircraft takes less of the impact than the front.
shots.scene: Remember the question? The tail.

items.s: FRONT TAKES MORE OF THE IMPACT

shots.line: Inside, the technology changed too. Early recorders used metal foil and magnetic tape, with moving parts that could break. Modern ones store everything on solid-state memory chips, like a much tougher version of the memory in your phone.
shots.scene: Tape to chips

shots.line: And even when the outside of a box is badly damaged, investigators can often remove the memory board, clean it, and read it directly in the lab. The armor only has to protect a tiny thing.
shots.scene: Damaged box: pull the memory board and read it

items.s: THE ARMOR PROTECTS A TINY THING

shots.line: For years, the cockpit voice recorder kept only the last two hours of sound, recording over the oldest audio again and again. Newer rules are pushing that to twenty-five hours, so investigators don't lose anything important that happened earlier in a long flight.
shots.scene: CVR: 2 hours, now 25 hours

shots.line: Another lesson came from accidents where the plane's electrical power failed, and the recorders went silent at exactly the wrong moment. Many newer cockpit recorders now carry their own small backup power supply, so they keep recording for around ten minutes after the plane's power is lost.
shots.scene: Backup power: ~10 more minutes

shots.line: There's one more piece. Bolted to each recorder is a small beacon. If it lands in water, it switches on and starts sending out a high-pitched ping, once every second, so search teams can hear it.
shots.scene: The underwater locator beacon pings

shots.line: But that beacon runs on a battery. And for one flight, that battery ran out long before anyone found it.
shots.scene: But the battery ran out

shots.line: Back to June two thousand nine. Ships race to the area where the plane went down, towing sensitive underwater microphones, listening for the pings.
shots.scene: June 2009: ships tow underwater microphones

shots.line: The problem is the ocean itself. The search area is huge, and the sea floor there is a landscape of underwater mountains and canyons, thousands of meters deep.
shots.scene: The sea floor: underwater mountains and canyons

shots.line: Searching it is like mowing a lawn in the dark. Ships tow sonar back and forth in long stripes, slowly painting a picture of the sea floor, strip by strip, looking for anything that doesn't belong.
shots.scene: Mowing the lawn in the dark: sonar stripes

items.s: LIKE MOWING A LAWN IN THE DARK

shots.line: The beacons are designed to ping for about thirty days. The searchers listen for weeks. They never hear them. And then the batteries go silent.
shots.scene: Beacon batteries: 30 days, then silence

shots.line: Search after search comes up empty. Months pass. Then a whole year. Then almost two.
shots.scene: Search after search: months, a year, almost two

shots.line: In two thousand eleven, a new search uses underwater robots, torpedo-shaped vehicles that glide just above the sea floor, scanning it with sonar, mile after mile.
shots.scene: 2011: robot subs glide above the floor with sonar

shots.line: The robots used in that search came from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in the United States, and they worked in shifts, diving for hours, surfacing, and diving again.
shots.scene: From Woods Hole, diving in shifts

shots.line: And finally, in April, almost two years after the crash, they find the debris field. Nearly four kilometers down.
shots.scene: April 2011: the debris field is found

shots.line: A remotely operated vehicle goes down, and lifts the recorders out of the mud.
shots.scene: An ROV lifts the recorders out of the mud

shots.line: After almost two years under crushing pressure, in the cold and the dark, the memory chips are carefully cleaned, dried, and read. And the data is there. Almost all of it.
shots.scene: In the lab: cleaned, dried, read. The data is there.

shots.line: There's a clever trick to that. Boxes recovered from the sea are often kept in water until they reach the lab, because drying out too fast can let salt and corrosion damage the electronics.
shots.scene: Keep it wet: recovered boxes stay in water

shots.line: Then comes the decoding. The raw data is just a stream of ones and zeros in the manufacturer's own format. Investigators translate it, check it against the plane's design, and turn it back into the flight.
shots.scene: Decoding: ones and zeros back into the flight

shots.line: Not every search ends like this. In two thousand fourteen, Malaysia Airlines flight three seventy disappeared with two hundred and thirty-nine people on board. Searchers combed a vast stretch of the Indian Ocean. Pieces of the plane eventually washed up on distant shores. But its recorders have never been found.
shots.scene: 2014: a flight that was never found

shots.line: And that changed the rules. Newer beacons now ping for ninety days instead of thirty. Airliners are being required to report their position more often over oceans. And engineers are working on recorders that eject and float, and systems that can stream key flight data live, before a plane ever hits the water.
shots.scene: New rules: 90-day beacons, tracking, eject & float, streaming

shots.line: But in two thousand eleven, in a lab in France, investigators finally pressed play. And for the first time, they heard what really happened that night.
shots.scene: 2011, France: investigators press play
